doc.title: Roy McCurdy interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Leaving Eastman Kodak to join Cannonball Adderley
summary: After sideman jobs he quit playing to save his marriage, worked at Kodak, then Cannon called to replace Louis Hayes.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: How did the thing with the Adderleys come about? Did you step in after, was it Louie Hayes?

Yeah. Well what had happened was I was in New York for a while, and I had played with the ‘tet and I’d played with Betty Carter and I had played with Mitchell and Ruff and Sonny Rollins. I had been with Sonny for quite a while. And then in 1960, no 63, I went back home. I was married, in my first marriage, and I was trying to save this marriage, © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-
and I went back to Rochester. And I took a job and I just stopped playing. I took a job at Eastman Kodak as a film tester.
I think half of Rochester worked at Eastman, and the other ones at Xerox.
Yeah. I was working in the dark and I had these big rolls of film, and listening to the jazz on the radio, hearing myself on albums and stuff.
Was that the Harry Abraham show?
Yeah. Actually, Harry Abraham, but at that time it was called Will Moyle.
Yeah. And you’re listening to yourself.

And I’m saying what am I doing here you know, in this place. And so it was about, I had been there almost a year and I got several calls, I mean Horace wanted me to come out and a couple of the other guys wanted me to come. And then this big chance came with Cannon. Louis Hayes was leaving to go with Oscar Peterson, and Cannon called and he said, I think his exact words were “Fool — I want you to come join my band.” So I said oh, man, what am I going to do about this? You know I was really tired of Kodak and so I talked to my wife and I told her that I was thinking about going. But I talked to the guys, the guys on the block that I grew up with and I told them. And they said if you don’t go, we’re going to — you’d better go. Because you know they’d been proud, I’d been playing with all these guys and we had grown up together and they knew it. So I told her “Listen, I’m going to go to New York” and I just went, and I joined Cannon. And it was great.
It took me about almost a month before my playing chops were back together, but he was very patient and it was great. And finally it just clicked and we had a good relationship.
